title: Let the children come (Mark 10:13–16)
hook: the disciples shoo away children, and he's indignant

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hard question about divorce, answered from the beginning. Your line was what god joined.

A waiting room. A toddler, a parent, and a person at the desk giving that look: keep the little one quiet and out of the way. Now the disciples wear that look. Parents are bringing their young children to Jesus, just so he'll touch them, and the disciples rebuke them and send them off. He's busy. He's important. There's serious talk going on about divorce and the Law. Take the kids home. Mark tells us how Jesus took it: when he saw it, he was much displeased. Not with the parents. Not with the children. With his friends.
screen: `PARENTS BRING THEIR LITTLE ONES.` → `THE DISCIPLES SEND THEM OFF.` → `HE'S MUCH DISPLEASED.`

segments.voice: Much displeased is the King James phrase. The Greek word is stronger: indignant. Matthew and Luke tell this story too, and both leave that part out. Mark keeps it. Then the words: "Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not: for of such is the kingdom of God." Suffer, in King James English, meant allow. Let them come. Then the line that turns it into a lesson for the grown-ups: whoever does not receive the kingdom of God as a little child will not enter it. How does a little child receive something? Watch a toddler handed a cookie. No negotiating, no asking what's the catch, no working out whether they've earned it. Hands open, and it's theirs. One way Christians hear the saying: the kingdom isn't a prize for the deserving, but a gift, for people willing to receive one. Mark ends the scene with three verbs: he took them up in his arms, put his hands on them, and blessed them. Not a pat on the head from a distance. Churches read this passage in different settings. Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican, Lutheran and Reformed churches baptize infants, and some read this passage at a baptism. Baptist and other churches baptize those old enough to profess faith, and some read it when parents bring a baby to be dedicated and blessed. Either way, the children end up in his arms.
screen: `ONLY MARK KEEPS HIS INDIGNATION.` · `SUFFER MEANS ALLOW.` · `RECEIVE IT LIKE A CHILD.` · `ARMS, HANDS, BLESSING.` · then, large: `FOR OF SUCH IS THE KINGDOM OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Notice one thing you've been given today that you didn't earn: the breath you're taking right now, sunlight, a message from someone, your own hands. Don't analyze it or ask whether you deserve it; just take it, the way a toddler takes a cookie, with open hands. If you pray, you can simply say thank you, like a child would.
Indignant, the strong word behind Jesus's anger when the disciples turned the children away. His lesson: receive the kingdom as a child receives a gift.
Your line: like a child. A gift is for receiving. Rest easy tonight.

howItsDone: Some churches that baptize infants read this passage at baptisms, and some churches that baptize believers read it at services where parents present a baby for dedication and blessing.

original.note: Greek: a little child, a small one. the word in Mark 10:13–15.

trapdoor: what you thought: a gentle picture of Jesus liking kids.
what it means: he is angry at his friends for shutting children out, and says the kingdom is received the way a child receives a gift.
what a scholar hears: of the three tellings, Mark alone keeps the indignation, aganakteō. and suffer is King James English for allow.

sources.quoted: Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not: for of such is the kingdom of God.

notes: 'Mark tells us something he tells us nowhere else': aganakteō is used of Jesus only here in the Gospels. Confirm.
Matthew 19:13–15 and Luke 18:15–17 omit Jesus's indignation. Confirm.
Baptism practices summarized by church family; confirm that this passage is commonly read at infant baptisms (e.g. traditional Anglican and Lutheran rites) and at dedications.
'Children then had no standing and nothing to trade' is a general social claim; confirm phrasing.
